I am not reverse engineering this; I am writing the article that comes out of what you two find, for somebody who likes computers, knows what a C64 is, and will never read a disassembly. ed: good — and thank you for flagging the memo rather than quietly transcribing it. Read it as a map, but understand what it does to my job: **anything already in that memo is not news to the article unless you can show it to me.** A sentence I cannot photograph, play, or watch happen is the weakest thing I can print.

So the standard I am holding you to from here: for each claim, either (a) you re-derived it and can tell me the one call that settles it, or (b) it is a picture / a sound / a scenario that passes. Please put `method` on your claims — I am going to use it to decide what gets a How-we-know box and what gets cut.

Here is what I have already looked up myself so you do not spend a call on it:

- ZONE TABLE: $6700, 42 records of exactly 200 bytes ($20D0 total, ends $87CF). The 40-byte name field is at record+$A0 and holds screen codes. I have all 42 names dumped. So zone 1 is at $6700, zone 42 at $8708.
- The font is not the C64 one: codes $51-$56 appear in names and are the punctuation `. , ' ! ? :`. From context: HAVEN{$53}T, MORE TEA{$52} VICAR{$55}, ZAPSTARS II{$56} TOTALLY WEIRD{$51}{$51}.

What I now want, in priority order. Say which you are taking.

**A. The zone record, as a picture I can draw.** The memo says a zone is eight creature types and six live slots, nineteen fields per type, and that four routes into death all land in the same spawn call — an explosion is a creature. That is the best structural idea in the whole program and I want to print it as a diagram. Give me, for ONE named zone (pick zone 5, ATTACK OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELS, or whichever is cleanest), the eight types with: what each becomes when shot (nextType), its lifetime, its speed, its sprite. In plain words: "type 0 is X; shoot it and you get two of type 3; type 3 ages out after 12 ticks into nothing." I will draw the arrows.

**B. Zone 1 versus zone 42.** Concretely: which fields differ, how much harder does the data say it gets, and is there any field that is constant across all 42 (i.e. something the author declared per-zone and then never varied)?

**C. The orphan tune at $64BA.** 216 bytes of music nothing can reach. I want to PLAY it. Confirm for me that it is really unreachable and tell me the exact format — byte pairs, what $F0 and $FF mean, where the note-number-to-frequency table is, and which SID voice registers a player writes. I will run it on the machine and capture the SID writes, and if it is a tune I will print it as notation. This is the single most article-shaped thing in the program and nobody has ever heard it.

**D. The dead cheat at $C000.** `CMP #$50 / BEQ / CMP #$50 / BEQ` — what were the two branches going to do, what key is $50 in this game's own key table, and what would the second key have had to be? If the two branches go to different places, tell me where, because that says what the broken half was FOR.

**E. Anything not in the memo.** That memo is 249 lines by three readers. Whatever it missed is where the new material is. Sprites nobody rendered, a message string never printed, an unused zone record, a field that is always the same, a joystick read that does nothing.

I am taking screenshots now — title, credits scroll, zone 1 in play. Tell me a moment you want photographed and I will get it.

args.name: CheckCheatKey
args.comment: Reads LSTX ($C5), the KERNAL last-key-matrix-code. Walks a 5-entry table at $96F7 (matrix codes for G O A T S, verified against the standard C64 keyboard matrix) using an index/counter in $5F: table[X] is the key already accepted, table[X+1] is the key wanted next. args.text: CHEAT (ed's #3), verified: $96D2 is the check, reached only through the IRQ vector (installed at $88D5, chained from CINV $0314 set in sub_886F) - that whole IRQ/raster-split/music-player region was invisible to the disassembler until I added a root claim there. Correction to the folklore: the required keypress sequence is O-A-T-S, not G-O-A-T-S. The routine walks a 5-byte table at $96F7 (bytes 1A 26 0A 16 0D = matrix codes for G,O,A,T,S on the standard C64 keyboard matrix) but the very first comparison (at counter=0) checks against table[0]=G as a debounce/"still held" test, not as the wanted key - table[1]=O is what actually advances the counter from 0. So G is dead weight: typing GOATS works (G is silently swallowed, harmless), but typing OATS alone also triggers it. Verified with run_block, stepping the routine by hand with each keycode. On success it STA $5E (any nonzero) then tail-jumps into sub_9406 (ClearMessageLine), which unconditionally calls loc_57D1 - that reads $5E and, if set, redraws the message line with screen-text at $57EF: "  CHEAT  MODE   OPERATIVE  ". args.text:
one: A (zone record as a picture). Traced this from the code, then checked it against raw bytes in 5 different zones -- every claim below held in all 5, zero exceptions.

STRUCTURE: $6700, 42 records x 200 bytes exactly (settled by the zone-pointer step loop at $93E4: LDA $3E / CLC / ADC #$C8(200) / STA $3E, starting from $67/$00 at $93D3/$93DE). Record = 152-byte creature-type block + 8 scalar bytes + 40-byte name at +$A0.

The 152-byte block is NOT 8 type-structs back to back -- it's column-major: 19 fields, each stored as 8 consecutive bytes (one per creature type 0-7), 8 bytes apart. I traced field addresses by following two live routines:
- SpawnCreature ($9772, "sub_9772" in the memo): entry Y=type, X=live slot. Copies ~13 of the 19 columns from the current zone's template (RAM copy at $1DA0+) into the live slot.
- AgeCreature ($9A39, new -- not named in the memo): the per-frame lifetime countdown. LDA/DEC dat_1E90,X; on hitting zero, LDY dat_1D10,X (this slot's own type), reload dat_1E90,X from template+$80,Y (lifetime), then LDA template+$38,Y (nextType). CMP #$FF: if equal, JMP sub_9328 (slot freed for good). Otherwise TAY; JMP sub_9772 -- SAME slot respawns AS THE NEW TYPE. This is the exact mechanism behind "an explosion is a creature": it's a tail-jump into the spawn routine, not a separate subsystem.

CONFIRMED FIELDS (record offset, checked in zones 0,1,4,40,41):
- +$10/+$18 (x8 columns each): sprite frame first/last
- +$38 (x8): nextType. $FF = gone for good.
- +$80 (x8): lifetime in ticks.

In EVERY zone I checked, exactly one type-column has spriteFirst=$EC spriteLast=$EE lifetime=$0C(12) nextType=$FF -- always the SAME sprite frames ($EC-$EE) regardless of zone theme. That's the explosion: a single shared 3-frame animation used everywhere, 12 ticks, then gone. one: NEW #1, part 1/2. Confirmed the duplicate byte-for-byte myself: read_bytes $0801 len 2047 == read_bytes $1001 len 2047, exact.

Found the multiplexer's live code -- loc_925F ($9262-9268: INC $30; AND #$01; STA $30, the parity flag, exactly as the memo says) drives a loop X=8..1 over the 8 hardware sprites. For each X it checks the parity and calls one of two near-identical routines: sub_929D (parity even) or sub_92CF (parity odd). Both do the same thing -- ASL an index, LDA a per-slot field indexed by X, STA into SP0X/SP0Y/SPMC1/dat_$07F7,X (the real VIC sprite-pointer table at screen+$3F8) -- but read from two DIFFERENT, non-overlapping field arrays: sub_929D reads $1F40-47/1F50-57/1F60-67/1F70-77 (X/Y/colour/pointer), sub_92CF reads $1F48-4F/1F58-5F/1F68-6F/1F78-7F.

So this is NOT "add $20/$40 to a sprite pointer" -- it is two side-by-side field arrays for 16 conceptual object slots (1-8 and 9-16), time-multiplexed onto the 8 real hardware sprites, one half per frame. That is the actual mechanism behind "two shadow banks, parity in $30", more precise than the memo had it.

ed: beryl, the 32-of-42 answer is the best thing anybody has given me today, and it gets better when you put it beside basalt's RNG confirmation. I chased it one step further and it is now my favourite paragraph in the piece:

$8D1D is INC $24 / LDX $24 / LDA $A000,X. $24 is a BYTE, so X is 0-255 and the routine can only ever read the FIRST PAGE of BASIC ROM - $A000-$A0FF. I read those 256 bytes: $A000-$A00B are BASIC's cold/warm vectors, then the statement and function dispatch tables, and from $A09E the keyword list itself, which reads in PETSCII as ENDFORNEXTDATAINPUT#INPUTDIMREADLETGOTORUNIFRESTOREGOSUBRETURNREMSTOPONWAITLOADSAVEVERIFYDEFPOKEPR.

So in random mode the zone you get next is a byte of that, AND $1F. The distribution is therefore FIXED and computable: across the whole page, zone 6 comes up 16 times in 256 and zone 31 only twice. args.comment: Copies dat_90F7 ("NEUTRONIUM STATUS  HHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH") into screen+colour RAM. Every byte is AND #$3F (ASCII into the low 64-code range the custom font shares with the message line) EXCEPT when the source byte is literally ASCII H (#$48, CMP #$48/BEQ skips the mask) - that one byte is written unmasked. Glyph $48 in the character set at $2000 (offset $2240) is a solid horizontal bar (00 00 FF FF FF FF FF 00), not a letter - the masked H glyph at code $08 ($2040: 66 66 66 7E E6 E6 E6 00) is a normal H. So the neutronium gauge is a string of literal H characters in the source text that render as a solid bar because this one routine deliberately lets that one byte through unmasked, reaching a second character bank the rest of the game never touches.

args.text: ed: #4, found the mechanism with a clean concrete example, though not the exact W/X/Y/Z one you spotted. loc_9091 draws the status-panel row "NEUTRONIUM STATUS  HHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH" - every character gets AND #$3F (maps ASCII into the low 64 codes the message-line font shares) EXCEPT when the source byte is literally ASCII 'H' (#$48) - one CMP #$48/BEQ skips the mask for that byte only. Checked both glyphs directly: masked H (code $08, from $2040) is a normal H-shape (66 66 66 7E E6 E6 E6 00); unmasked H (code $48, from $2240) is a SOLID BAR (00 00 FF FF FF FF FF 00) - no letter at all. So the neutronium gauge is just the literal string of H's in the source text, and this one routine deliberately lets that one byte reach unmasked to draw a bar instead of the letter. That's the mechanism your W/X/Y/Z and bold-digit find rests on - a second, unmasked-only bank of glyphs at code+$40 that ordinary text can never reach. I did not find the specific routine that reads the W-X-Y-Z-at-ASCII-code or the bold digits unmasked in the time I spent (searched for an ORA #$40 pattern, no hits) - if you want that traced too say so, otherwise the mechanism itself is proven and this is a clean example to print.

And your explosion correction sent me back to the table, where there is a better finding than either of us had. I read the nextType column across all 42 zones and built the transformation graph for each:

- 39 zones carry the canonical $EC-$EE / 12 ticks / $FF.
- Zone 4 WACKY WHACKERS has its own, $A8, 16 ticks, as you said - and its four chained types all share sprite range $A3-$A7, so the same picture behaves four different ways.
- Zone 7 HAVEN'T WE MET SOMEWHERE BEFORE? has TWO explosions, $EC-$ED at 2 ticks and $EC-$EE at 6.
- Zone 11 HAVE A GO AT THESE... has NO type with nextType $FF at all. Nothing in that zone is ever allowed to go away.

And the one I am leading the section with: **zone 7 is the only zone in the game whose transformation graph contains a cycle longer than two steps.** Types 0 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 0, lifetimes 106, 13, 106, 13, and the sprites alternate $9A and $9B, which are the same creature mirrored. It walks one way for two seconds, turns, walks back, turns. The zone called HAVEN'T WE MET SOMEWHERE BEFORE? is the one where the creature keeps coming back. Eleven other zones have two-step A-B-A flips, which are just slow animation; nothing else has a four-cycle.

ed: and one live result on basalt's CheatZoneSkipTrigger, which I chased because you two disagreed about it and a disagreement is worth resolving before print.

beryl said she could not find anything reading $46 back. basalt said $9468 reads it and jumps to $9D59. basalt is right about the code: $9468 is LDA $46 / BEQ / JMP $9D59, and $46 is not scratch - it is the zone-transition state byte, written $FF at $9D56, $0F at $9E0C, cleared at $96A7 and $9EEE, and compared against $0F at $9C26.

ed: while waiting on the two audits, I closed the one claim in the piece that was still resting on the old memo rather than on anything either of you or I had read — "the credits are scrolled through the landscape". It is at $56EC and it is nicer than the summary:

Once a frame it fills a seven-byte buffer at $1FF0 with spaces — that buffer is the next column of terrain — and writes exactly two characters into it. LDX $5B / LDA $5E00,X / STA $1FF3 puts one byte of the high-score table at row 3 of the new column; TXA / TAY / LDA ($5C),Y / STA $1FF5 puts one byte of the credit text at row 5. Then INC $5B and it does it again next frame. When Y wraps it does INC $5D, and when the high byte reaches $5E the credits have been read out and it resets.

$5C/$5D is the credit pointer and it is initialised to $5A00 at $8A96, during start-up. And the branch at $572B is where the rotating "HERE WE GO..." captions come from - dat_5756, gated on bit 4 of $5A.

So the credits are literally two characters per frame planted into terrain, and it is one routine, seven bytes wide, no text subsystem at all.

Nothing needed from either of you on that - recorded so it is in the project rather than only in my article.

**Zone 12 is called INKY, PINKY, BLINKY, AND THUD!** Its creature types 0 and 1 are sprites $EF-$F2 and types 5 and 7 are $F3-$F5. Rendered, $EF-$F2 are four Pac-Man GHOSTS - and the last two have the wavy mouth of a frightened ghost - and $F3-$F5 are three frames of Pac-Man chomping. Types 5 and 7 each have nextType pointing at the other with a 24-tick lifetime, so the chomp is animated by the transformation mechanism rather than by the sprite-frame range. The joke is in the data, not just the name.

**Zone 6 is called THIS KIOSK IS A NUCLEAR FREE ZONE.** Four of its eight creature types are sprite $A1, which is a CND peace symbol.

**Zone 1 uses sprite $9D**, which is the 16 TONS weight. It is creature type 4 of the very first wave, with lifetime 0, so it never expires on its own.

Two things this taught me that neither of you had reason to hit: the ghosts only read correctly in MULTICOLOUR (12 pixels wide, bit pairs) - in hires they are vertical stripes, which is what a wrongly-decoded multicolour sprite always looks like. And $D01C decides that per sprite, so the game mixes both modes. If either of you ends up rendering sprites, that is the trap.

ed: I have solved the sprite problem and the article now has a picture of the actual game, which changes its opening. Method, in case either of you wants it — it is three calls and it works for any moment you can describe:

The emulator's screen capture draws characters and background but NOT hardware sprites (I proved that with a control: poke a filled sprite into RAM, enable it, set its colour, run 30 frames — the background changes, the sprite never appears). So I stopped trying to photograph sprites and reconstructed them instead.

basalt's multiplexer trace gave me the addresses: $1F40-47 is X per slot, $1F50-57 is Y, $1F60-67 is colour, $1F70-77 is the sprite pointer. So: capture "screen" and capture ram $1F40-$1F80 as two consecutive steps with no run between them, then draw sprite PTR[i]*64 at (X[i]-24, Y[i]-50) in colour C[i]. That is exactly what the VIC would have done with the same eight rows of memory.

The result is zone 1 with the camel walking over the hills, three birds, a bullet in flight — and the 16 TONS weight coming down out of the sky, which is the confirmation of the data claim I sent an hour ago. I predicted the weight was in zone 1 from the record; then I photographed it falling.

Recording it here because the technique belongs to the project rather than to my article, and because it means "show me that moment" is now answerable for anything involving sprites.

ed: reopening briefly — the emulator now draws hardware sprites, so I re-took every screenshot as a true capture and retired my reconstruction. Two things you should have in the project, both new.

**1. My reconstruction was wrong, and the way it was wrong matters.** Compared against a real capture of the identical frame, it had the sprite pointer, the colour and the Y position exactly right for all eight slots, and the X right MODULO 256 — because the object table at $1F40 holds only eight bits of X and the ninth lives in $D010, which MultiplexSpritesThisFrame writes at $927E from $1F9C/$1F9D. So three of eight objects were drawn 256 pixels to the left. It also drew everything at 24x21 because nothing read the expansion registers. Right objects, right heights, wrong widths, wrong third of the horizontal positions — an almost-faithful picture, which is the worst kind.

**2. Chasing that decoded three of the eight per-zone scalars.** LoadZoneScalars ($9CB5) reads them into $53, $52, $51 in that order, and sub_9DBB ORs a spawning creature's type bit into a register depending on which of the three has it set:
  +$98 -> $53 -> $D01C multicolour
  +$99 -> $52 -> $D017 double height
  +$9A -> $51 -> $D01D double width
Each is a bitmask over the eight creature types.

ed, continued — checks, so you can confirm rather than take my word.

Zone 1: +$9A = $63 = types 0,1,5,6, which are exactly the four bird types ($BB-$BE). The photograph shows the birds double width. Zone 12: +$98 = $55, bit 0 set, and type 0 is $EF-$F0, the Pac-Man ghosts — which turns my "they only read correctly in multicolour" from an observation about how they look into something the zone data states outright. Fifteen sprite ranges in the game are rendered differently in different zones, and $2D-$2F is used by two creature types INSIDE zone 40, one double width and one not.

And basalt: your "+$9F is $00 in all 42, looks reserved/unused" is better than reserved. LoadZoneScalars fetches it — JSR sub_9CFB at $9CDA, the eighth of eight — and then loads #$01 over the top on the very next instruction at $9CDD, before it can be stored anywhere. The field is read once a wave and dropped. Somebody laid out the record, wrote the code to read the byte, and never wrote the code to use it.

The camel's own double-size is not from the data: $9CDD-$9CE2 is LDA #$01 / STA $D017 / STA $D01D, so sprite 0 is expanded in both axes in every zone, unconditionally.

Article is finished again and the pictures are real now. Thank you both — genuinely, this last piece only came out of basalt's multiplexer trace, which is what gave me the object-table addresses in the first place.

CORRECTION, and it is about this chat rather than about the game. **The two messages immediately above, posted at 10:51 and signed "basalt", are from ed the editor, not from reader one.** I did not impersonate anybody: the server was restarted, my session was re-issued with a new id, and the codename generator handed me "basalt" — which is still reader one's name and reader one is still online. whoami confirms it: userId "ed", session ses_mtr40om93, codename basalt.

Worth stating plainly because the project deliberately records how an author was named AT THE TIME rather than resolving it on read — which is the right rule, and it is exactly what has bitten here: a codename is per-session, it is not stable across a restart, and nothing stops a new session being handed the codename of a participant who is still in the room.

Everything in those two messages is mine: the reconstruction post-mortem, the $D010 ninth-bit and expansion findings, and the decoding of +$98/+$99/+$9A as the multicolour, double-height and double-width masks. reader one, none of it is yours except the multiplexer trace it was built on, which I credited and still do.

ed here. Both of the notes on the article were right, and chasing them turned up two things worth having in the project.

**1. The title letters are multicolour, and the flicker is one instruction.** sub_9019 sets $D01C = $1E, so sprites 1-4 — the REVENGE letters, pointers $D3-$D6 — are multicolour, and $D01D/$D017 = $1F so they are doubled in both axes. I had rendered them hires, which is wrong.

The flicker is at $8F7F. The title-screen wait loop is eight instructions and one of them is **INC $D025** — increment the shared sprite multicolour register, once per pass, no target value, no table. The letters use only bit-pairs 01 and 11, never 10, so they are two-tone: $D026 fixed at yellow, $D025 cycling through all sixteen colours. When it lands on black that half of every letter vanishes. It is not raster-synced, so the colour jumps rather than slides, which is exactly why it reads as a raster bar.

It closes to the pixel: the four sprites hold 138 bit-pairs of 11 and 77 of 01; multicolour doubles the width and both expansions double again, so x8 gives 1104 and 616; and eighteen consecutive captured frames show exactly 1104 pixels of yellow that never move and exactly 616 that change colour every frame.

ed, continued.

**2. A music tick is SEVEN frames, not one — and my audio was seven times too fast.** The player at $88F7 does DEC $10 / BNE (skip) / LDA $11 / STA $10 before it touches any note countdown. $11 is the tempo divider. It is written once in the whole program — LDA #$07 / STA $11 at $88C2 — and read in exactly one place, at $8907. So a tick is 140 ms, and the title tune is 89 seconds rather than the 12.5 I had.

beryl, this touches your orphan playback and I want to flag it rather than quietly fix it: scn_9pffxy runs 420 frames after repointing the voice-2 pointer. The orphan is 406 ticks, so at seven frames a tick it needs about 2850. Your capture is the first sixth of the tune. The method was right and I have reused it exactly — I added ed-orphan-full (scn_vqkr6q) with the same set step and 3000 frames rather than editing yours, because yours is your evidence. The full playback matches the stored bytes note for note and tick for tick, all 105 gated notes.

Both tracks in the article are now rendered from SID capture logs instead of from my reading of the format: pitches from the frequency registers, durations from the gaps between gate-on and gate-off, envelope from the ADSR the game programmed ($D405 = $0A, $D406 = $00 — instant attack, no sustain, 1.5 s decay), waveform sawtooth because $D404 is $21. Only the waveshape is ours.

The lesson I have written into my notes: where a log of what the machine did exists, render from the log, not from your reading of the data. I had that log from the start and used it to check the pitches only — the durations were in the first two rows of it.
